cases.observation: The attacking midfielder plays a first-time through ball down the right channel. At the moment the ball leaves the passer's foot, the receiving forward's leading foot, torso and head are level with the second-last defender's torso, with the two players' shoulders in line and no daylight between them along the line across the pitch. The forward then accelerates past the defender, takes one touch and drives into the area. Both the forward and the second-last defender are fully in frame at the moment the pass is struck. The assistant referee's flag goes up as the forward reaches the ball.
cases.rationale: Law 11.1 requires part of the head, body or feet to be nearer to the opponents' goal line than the second-last opponent. The observation puts the forward level with, not nearer than, that defender, so no offside position existed and the flag was wrong.

cases.observation: A midfielder inside his own half slides a pass forward through the defensive line. At the moment the ball is played the forward is standing roughly two metres beyond the second-last defender, well inside the opponents' half, with only the goalkeeper nearer to the goal line than him. The forward runs onto the pass, takes a touch and shoots at goal. All three players and the halfway line are clearly in frame at the moment of the pass. The assistant referee raises the flag as the forward takes his first touch.
cases.rationale: Law 11.1: the forward was in the opponents' half and nearer to the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent when the ball was played, so he was in an offside position and the flag was correct.

cases.observation: A cross is struck from the left wing. A second attacker is standing beyond the second-last defender near the far post at the moment the cross is played, but he stays rooted with his arms at his sides and never moves toward the ball or toward any opponent. The ball travels past him untouched to a team-mate who was level with the defensive line, and that team-mate heads it into the net. No defender is within three metres of the stationary attacker and he is not between the goalkeeper and the ball at any point. The assistant's flag goes up after the header crosses the line.
cases.rationale: Law 11.2 penalises a player in an offside position only on becoming involved in active play by playing or touching the ball or interfering with an opponent. The stationary attacker did neither, so no offence occurred and the flag was wrong.

cases.observation: A forward strikes a shot from the edge of the area. At the moment the shot is struck, a second forward is standing clearly beyond the second-last defender, roughly three metres nearer to the goal line. The ball hits the inside of the near post and rebounds back across the six-yard box to that second forward, who side-foots it into the empty net. The post, both forwards and the second-last defender are all in frame at the moment the shot is struck. No flag is raised, no whistle sounds and the goal stands.
cases.rationale: No call was made and the goal was allowed to stand. Law 11.2 (gaining an advantage) penalises a player in an offside position who plays a ball that has rebounded off the goalpost, so the goal should have been disallowed and allowing it was wrong.

cases.observation: A midfielder shoots from twenty metres. At the moment the shot is struck a forward is standing two metres beyond the second-last defender, directly ahead of the ball. The goalkeeper dives and parries the shot with both hands, pushing it out to the side. The offside-positioned forward runs onto the parried ball and rolls it into the empty net. The goalkeeper's two-handed save and the forward's starting position are both clearly visible in frame. The flag goes up and the goal is disallowed.
cases.rationale: Law 11.2 (gaining an advantage) expressly covers a ball that has been deliberately saved by an opponent. The forward was in an offside position and played the rebound from the goalkeeper's save, so disallowing the goal was correct.

cases.observation: A defender clears the ball long downfield. At the moment the ball is struck the target forward is standing inside his own half; the halfway line and centre circle are clearly painted in frame and both of his feet are on the defensive side of the line. He then runs forward, controls the ball on his chest in the opponents' half and drives at goal. The second-last defender is several metres upfield of him at the moment of the clearance. The assistant raises the flag as the forward takes his first touch.
cases.rationale: Law 11.1 requires part of the head, body or feet to be in the opponents' half for an offside position to exist. The forward was entirely in his own half when the ball was played, so the flag was wrong.

cases.observation: A winger carries the ball to the byline and cuts it backwards toward the penalty spot. At the moment he plays the ball, the arriving striker is roughly four metres further from the goal line than the ball, so the pass travels backwards, away from goal. Only the goalkeeper is nearer to the goal line than the striker at that instant. The striker meets the cut-back first time and scores. The ball, the winger and the striker are all in frame at the moment the pass is played, and the flag goes up as the shot is struck.
cases.rationale: Law 11.1 requires a player to be nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. The striker was behind the ball when it was played, so no offside position existed regardless of the defenders' positions.

cases.observation: The camera is zoomed tight on the passer as he strikes a through ball, so only his boot and the ball are inside the frame at the moment of contact. The shot widens roughly a second later, by which point the forward is already running clear with the second-last defender trailing several metres behind him. Because the defensive line was entirely outside the frame at the moment the ball was played, the relative positions of the forward and the second-last defender at that instant are not shown anywhere in the clip. The forward goes on to round the goalkeeper as the flag is raised.
cases.rationale: Law 11.1 turns entirely on the players' relative positions at the moment the ball is played, and that frame is outside the camera's field of view. No rule can be established, so the observation cannot decide the call.

cases.observation: A midfielder clips a ball over the top of the defence. At the moment of contact the striker's leading shoulder and both feet are in line with the second-last defender's trailing foot, the two players level along the line across the pitch with neither body ahead of the other. The striker takes one touch, advances and finishes past the goalkeeper. Both the striker and the second-last defender are fully in frame at the moment the pass is struck. No flag is raised, no whistle sounds and the goal is given.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play was allowed to continue. Law 11.1 penalises a player only if part of him is nearer to the goal line than the second-last opponent; level is not nearer, so there was no offside position and letting the goal stand was correct.

cases.observation: A shot is struck from twenty metres. At the moment the ball leaves the boot, a forward is standing about a metre beyond the second-last defender, directly in front of the goalkeeper and inside his line of sight. As the ball travels, the forward stretches his leg out toward it and jumps, and the goalkeeper visibly checks his dive and shifts his weight sideways to avoid him. The ball passes between the forward's legs untouched and goes into the net. The flag goes up and the goal is disallowed.
cases.rationale: Law 11.2 penalises a player in an offside position who becomes involved in active play by interfering with an opponent. The forward attempted to play the ball from an offside position and made the goalkeeper alter his dive, so disallowing the goal was correct.

cases.observation: The attacker knocks the ball a metre ahead of himself down the touchline. The defender slides in from the side with his leading leg extended and the sole of his boot angled toward the ground; his instep makes contact with the ball first and the ball is knocked clearly away toward the touchline. His leg then continues through and his shin contacts the attacker's trailing leg, and the attacker trips over him and falls. The contact with the ball and the subsequent contact with the leg are both clearly visible in frame, and the defender's studs never rise above ankle height. The referee blows and awards a free kick to the attacking side.
cases.originalCall: foul - free kick to the attacking side
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 (Fair Tackle) states a tackle is fair if the defender contacts the ball before the attacker, and that unavoidable subsequent contact after winning the ball cleanly is generally not a foul. The observation shows exactly that, with no carelessness, recklessness or excessive force, so the free kick was wrong.

cases.observation: Two players arrive at a loose ball in midfield at the same time. The defender gets there marginally first and pokes the ball away with the outside of his right boot; the ball is visibly moving away before the two players meet. They then collide shoulder to shoulder and the attacker stumbles and goes to ground. Neither player raises a foot and there is no studs contact at any point. No whistle sounds and play continues with a third player collecting the loose ball.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play continued. Law 12.1 (Fair Tackle) treats a challenge in which the ball is contacted first, with no carelessness or force, as no foul, so playing on was correct.

cases.observation: The attacker takes a touch past the defender in midfield. The defender slides in from behind with his leading leg extended; the ball is already a full stride beyond his reach and his boot does not touch it at any point in the sequence. His shin makes contact with the attacker's standing ankle and the attacker is tripped and falls forward. The ball runs on untouched to a team-mate. The defender's studs stay down and the slide is at moderate speed with no lunge. The referee whistles and awards a free kick against the defender, showing no card.
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 (Careless) gives the example of tripping an opponent by missing the ball, and states no disciplinary sanction is needed. A direct free kick with no card is exactly the correct outcome.

cases.observation: The attacker shields the ball near the touchline. The defender lunges in from the side with one leg extended and the studs of his boot showing at roughly ankle height. He misses the ball entirely and the studs strike the front of the attacker's ankle, knocking him off his feet. The defender's momentum carries him past the ball without touching it. The point of contact on the ankle is clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles, awards a free kick and shows a yellow card.
cases.originalCall: foul - free kick and yellow card
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 (Reckless) gives the example of a sliding tackle with studs showing that hits the opponent's ankle or foot, and requires a direct free kick plus a caution. The free kick and yellow card match the rule.

cases.observation: The defender sprints in from four metres away and leaves the ground with both feet, studs first, at high speed. He misses the ball entirely and his studs strike the attacker's shin roughly a hand's width above the ankle, visibly bending the leg sideways at the point of impact. The attacker is thrown to the ground and stays down holding the leg. The height of the contact on the shin and the defender's speed into the challenge are both clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles, awards a free kick and shows a yellow card.
cases.originalCall: foul - free kick and yellow card
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 (Excessive Force) covers a high-speed lunge with studs striking above the ankle and states the player must be sent off. The foul itself was correctly given but the sanction was a caution rather than the required red card, so the call was wrong.

cases.observation: The defender charges in at full speed and jumps into the challenge with his leading leg straight and the studs raised above the height of the ball. He makes no contact with the ball at any point; the studs land on the attacker's shin well above the ankle and rake down it. The attacker is knocked backwards and remains on the ground. The height of the studs relative to the ball is clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles immediately and shows a red card.
cases.originalCall: foul - free kick and red card
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 (Excessive Force) describes a high-speed lunge with studs striking above the ankle as exceeding necessary force and endangering the opponent's safety, requiring a sending-off. The red card was correct.

cases.observation: The attacker plays the ball away with the inside of his foot. The defender arrives roughly half a second later at jogging pace with his foot low and the studs pointing down at the grass; his toe clips the attacker's ankle from the front and the attacker stumbles forward and falls. There is no lunge and no raised foot, and the defender is visibly slowing as he makes contact. The attacker gets straight back to his feet. The referee whistles, awards a free kick and shows a yellow card.
cases.originalCall: foul - free kick and yellow card
cases.rationale: A late, low-speed, studs-down contact after the ball has gone shows a lack of attention rather than disregard for the opponent's safety, which is careless under Law 12.1 (Careless). That rule states no disciplinary sanction is needed, so the caution made the call wrong.

cases.observation: The attacker drives toward the penalty area with the defender alongside him. As the defender extends his leg into the challenge, a third player runs directly between the camera and the two players, and both the ball and the players' legs are fully hidden for the entire duration of the contact. When the third player clears the frame the attacker is already on the ground and the ball is spinning away. Whether the defender's boot reached the ball before it reached the attacker's leg is not visible from this angle in any frame. The referee whistles and awards a free kick.
cases.rationale: The whole question is whether the ball was played first (Law 12.1 Fair Tackle) or missed (Law 12.1 Careless), and the moment of contact is physically blocked by a third player. No rule can be established from the observation.

cases.observation: Both players slide for a fifty-fifty ball in midfield. The defender arrives at speed with his leading leg fully extended and his studs up; his boot reaches the ball a fraction before the attacker's and the ball squirts sideways out of the challenge. His leg continues through at the same speed and the studs strike the attacker's shin a hand's width above the ankle, spinning him to the ground where he stays down. The defender's second leg is also off the ground throughout the challenge. The contact with the ball and the follow-through onto the shin are both clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles and shows a red card.
cases.originalCall: foul - free kick and red card
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 (Fair Tackle) makes a ball-first tackle fair only if it is not careless, reckless or using excessive force. A high-speed, two-footed, studs-up follow-through onto the shin above the ankle endangers safety under Law 12.1 (Excessive Force), so the red card was correct despite the ball being touched first.

cases.observation: The attacker takes a touch past the defender inside the penalty area; the painted penalty-area line is clearly visible in frame and both players are several metres inside it. The defender slides in, misses the ball completely, and his trailing leg catches the attacker's standing foot, tripping him to the ground. The ball rolls harmlessly through to the goalkeeper. The defender's studs remain on the turf and there is no lunge. The referee whistles and points to the penalty spot.
cases.rationale: Tripping an opponent by missing the ball is a direct free kick offence, and Law 14.1 states a penalty kick is awarded when a direct free kick offence is committed inside the offender's own penalty area. The contact is shown clearly inside the painted line.

cases.observation: The attacker is running diagonally toward goal when the defender clips his heels from behind and he goes to ground. The camera is high and behind the goal, and a cluster of players stands between the lens and the painted penalty-area line, so no part of that line is visible near the point of contact. The attacker's first stumble and his landing are two to three metres apart along his line of travel. Whether the contact occurred inside or outside the penalty area cannot be determined from this angle. The referee points to the penalty spot.
cases.rationale: A trip clearly occurred, but the disputed question is whether it happened inside the penalty area, which is what Law 14.1 turns on. The penalty-area line is occluded at the point of contact, so the restart cannot be decided and no rule is established.

cases.observation: The attacker carries the ball into the final third with the defender tracking alongside him. The defender stretches out his right leg and nicks the ball away from the attacker's feet with the toe of his boot; the ball is clearly struck first and rolls away to a team-mate. The attacker's trailing leg then catches the defender's planted foot and he tumbles over. The defender's studs stay on the ground throughout and he does not lunge or leave his feet. No whistle sounds and play continues.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play continued. Law 12.1 (Fair Tackle) states that where the defender wins the ball cleanly and subsequent unavoidable contact occurs it is generally not a foul, so playing on was correct.

cases.observation: The defender is sprinting back toward his own goal at full stride when a deflected ball comes at him from four metres away. His arms are swinging in the normal running motion, elbows bent and hands passing close to his hips, with the near forearm roughly a hand's width from his ribs at the moment of impact. The ball strikes that forearm and rebounds away. His silhouette is no wider than that of any player running at that speed, and the arm does not move toward the ball at any point. The referee whistles and awards a free kick.
cases.rationale: The handball exceptions state it is not an offence if the hand or arm is close to the body and does not make the body unnaturally bigger. The arm was in the natural running position close to the ribs and did not move toward the ball, so the free kick was wrong.

cases.observation: A free kick is struck toward a four-man defensive wall. As the ball is hit, the player at the end of the wall jumps and raises both arms straight above his head, well clear of his shoulders and away from his torso. The ball strikes his raised right hand and deflects away for a corner. The arms remain extended upward and outward throughout the jump, roughly doubling the width of his blocking silhouette. The referee whistles and awards a free kick.
cases.rationale: Raising both arms above the head in a wall is not a consequence of, or justifiable by, the body movement for that situation, so under the 'unnaturally bigger' rule the contact is an offence and the free kick was correct.

cases.observation: A cross is driven in hard from the right. It strikes the thigh of a defender standing at the near post and ricochets sideways over a distance of roughly one metre onto the upper arm of a second defender standing immediately beside him. That second defender's arm is tucked against his ribs with the elbow bent and pressed to his side, and there is no visible reaction time between the deflection and the contact. The ball drops to the ground and is cleared. Both defenders and the deflection off the thigh are clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles and points to the penalty spot.
cases.rationale: The handball exceptions state it is not an offence if the ball touches the arm directly from the head or body of another player who is close, and the arm here was also tucked against the body. The penalty was wrong.

cases.observation: The defender turns his body to block a shot from close range. The ball strikes his own thigh first and pops upward off it. It travels perhaps forty centimetres and then hits his own upper arm, which is folded across his chest with the hand tucked under the opposite armpit. The ball drops at his feet and he clears it upfield. The sequence of thigh then arm is clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles and awards a free kick.
cases.rationale: The handball exceptions state it is not an offence if the ball touches the arm directly from the player's own body, and additionally the arm was folded close to the chest rather than making the body bigger. The free kick was wrong.

cases.observation: A midfielder is beaten by a lofted pass over his head. He turns, reaches up and out with his right arm fully extended above his shoulder, and pushes the ball down out of the air with an open palm. The arm travels upward toward the ball while the ball is still a metre away from him. The ball drops at his feet and he plays it on. The arm movement toward the ball is clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles and awards a free kick.
cases.rationale: The deliberate handling rule covers a player moving the hand or arm towards the ball. The arm was raised toward the ball before contact and the ball was pushed down with an open palm, so the free kick was correct.

cases.observation: The defender slides across to block a cross inside the penalty area, with the painted line clearly visible behind him, and ends up on the ground. As he lands, his left hand is planted flat on the turf directly beneath his shoulder, taking his body weight and holding his chest off the grass. The ball, deflected off an attacker's boot two metres away, strikes that planted hand while it is still bearing his weight against the ground. The hand does not move toward the ball and stays flat on the turf throughout. The referee whistles and points to the penalty spot.
cases.rationale: The handball exceptions state it is not an offence when a player falls and the hand or arm is between the body and the ground to support the body. The hand was weight-bearing on the turf at the moment of contact, so the penalty was wrong.

cases.observation: The defender slides in to block a shot from the edge of the penalty area, with the painted line visible in frame. As he slides, his right arm is extended horizontally out from his shoulder at roughly chest height and clear of the ground, with the hand a full arm's length from his torso, while his left hand alone is on the turf supporting him. The ball strikes the raised right forearm and deflects away for a corner. The extended arm roughly doubles the width he covers as he slides. No whistle sounds and the corner kick is taken.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play continued. With the other hand already supporting the slide, an arm held horizontally at chest height is not justifiable by the body movement for that situation, so under the 'unnaturally bigger' rule an offence occurred and should have been penalised.

cases.observation: A low cross is fired into a crowded goalmouth. The defender turns his back to the ball a fraction before it arrives, so his torso is directly between the camera and the point of impact. The ball changes direction sharply off his right side, but whether it struck his hip, his flank or his upper arm is hidden behind his body from this angle. His right arm is not visible in any frame from the moment of contact onward. The referee whistles and points to the penalty spot.
cases.rationale: Every handball rule turns on whether the ball touched the hand or arm and on the arm's position, and both are physically hidden by the defender's own body. No rule can be established from the observation.

cases.observation: A cross is floated toward the far post. The attacker rises alongside the goalkeeper and, as the ball comes down, drives his closed right fist upward and outward into it; the arm extends toward the ball from a bent position, separately from his jumping motion. The ball changes direction sharply off the fist and goes into the net. The punching motion is clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles, disallows the goal and awards a free kick to the defending side.
cases.rationale: The deliberate handling rule covers a player moving the hand or arm towards the ball. Punching the ball with a closed fist is a clear deliberate touch, so disallowing the goal was correct.

cases.observation: A shot is struck from six metres out. The defender turns his body and head away from the ball to protect his face, bringing both arms in behind his back with the hands crossed at the base of his spine. The ball strikes the back of one forearm where it rests against his lower back. His arms leave his silhouette no wider than his torso and neither arm moves toward the ball. No whistle sounds and play continues as the ball runs out for a throw-in.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play continued. The handball exceptions state it is not an offence if the hand or arm is close to the body and does not make the body unnaturally bigger; arms tucked behind the back satisfy that, so playing on was correct.

cases.observation: The attacker knocks the ball past the defender near the corner of the penalty area. The defender extends his leg toward the ball but pulls it back, and a gap of roughly half a metre remains between his boot and the attacker's legs throughout. The attacker then throws both legs up behind him and lands face down. No part of either player touches the other at any point in the sequence, and both players' legs are unobstructed in frame. The referee whistles, shows the attacker a yellow card and awards a free kick to the defending side.
cases.originalCall: simulation - yellow card to the attacker
cases.rationale: Law 12.3 requires that pretending to have been fouled be sanctioned as unsporting behaviour with a yellow card. The observation shows a visible gap and no contact, so the caution was correct.

cases.observation: The attacker pushes the ball forward into the channel and accelerates. The defender, recovering from behind, swings his trailing leg through and his boot catches the attacker's standing ankle from the side; the attacker's foot is visibly knocked out from under him and his leg folds inward before he goes down. The defender's boot does not touch the ball, which runs on ahead. The contact on the ankle and the deflection of the attacker's leg are both clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles, shows the attacker a yellow card for simulation and awards a free kick to the defending side.
cases.originalCall: simulation - yellow card to the attacker
cases.rationale: There was real contact: the defender missed the ball and knocked the attacker's standing leg away, which is the careless challenge described in Law 12.1 (Careless). Nothing was feigned, so cautioning the attacker for simulation and giving the free kick the other way was wrong.

cases.observation: The attacker runs into the penalty area, with the painted line visible in frame, and cuts across the defender's path. The defender turns and jogs alongside him with both hands held behind his back and his feet planted wide; at no point does any part of him reach the attacker, and clear daylight is visible between the two throughout. The attacker throws his head back, flings out both arms and falls to the turf. The ball runs through to the goalkeeper. No whistle sounds, no card is shown and play continues.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play continued. Law 12.3 requires that pretending to have been fouled be sanctioned as unsporting behaviour punishable by a yellow card, so allowing the clear dive to go unpunished was wrong.

cases.observation: The attacker cuts inside the defender at the top of the penalty area. The defender is directly between the camera and the attacker at the moment the attacker falls, so the attacker's trailing leg and the defender's near leg are completely hidden behind the defender's body. The attacker's upper body pitches forward and he lands on his side. From this angle it cannot be seen whether the defender's leg made contact with the attacker's at any point. The referee whistles and shows the attacker a yellow card.
cases.originalCall: simulation - yellow card to the attacker
cases.rationale: Law 12.3 applies only if the attacker was pretending, which requires knowing that no contact occurred, and the legs are physically blocked by the defender's body. No rule can be established from the observation.

cases.observation: The attacker turns into the penalty area and goes to ground as the defender steps across him. A second defender and the goalkeeper are between the camera and the two players for the whole of the contact, and the attacker's legs disappear from view about half a second before he lands. When the players clear the frame the attacker is already down and the ball has run through to the goal line. Whether the defender's leg or body touched him is not visible from this angle. No whistle sounds and play continues.
cases.rationale: No call was made, but the observation cannot establish whether there was contact, a foul or simulation because the players are occluded through the decisive moment. No rule can be established.

cases.observation: A ball is knocked into the space behind the defence. As the attacker sets off, a defender who is not playing the ball steps directly across his running line and braces his forearm and shoulder into the attacker's chest. The two make firm body contact, the attacker is pushed off his line and has to break stride, and neither player is within playing distance of the ball at that moment. The contact between the forearm and the chest is clearly visible in frame. The referee whistles and signals an indirect free kick, holding one arm above his head.
cases.rationale: Impeding an opponent with contact is a direct free kick offence under Law 12.1, whereas the indirect free kick under Law 12.2 applies only when no contact is made. Contact is clearly shown, so the indirect restart was wrong.

cases.observation: A through ball is played down the middle. A defender who is nowhere near the ball moves sideways into the attacker's running line and shortens his stride, staying in front of him for two or three steps. The attacker has to check his run and slow down to avoid him, and clear daylight remains between the two players throughout, with no part of either touching the other. The ball runs on to the goalkeeper. The referee whistles and signals a direct free kick, pointing straight ahead toward the goal.
cases.rationale: Law 12.2 states that impeding the progress of an opponent without any contact is punished with an indirect free kick. The observation shows no contact at all, so awarding a direct free kick was the wrong restart.

cases.observation: A loose ball rolls toward the touchline, four or five metres away from both players. A defender steps into the attacker's path and side-steps twice to stay in front of him as the attacker tries to go around, blocking his route to the ball. Neither player touches the other at any point and a visible gap is maintained throughout. The defender never attempts to play the ball and is never within playing distance of it. The referee whistles and signals an indirect free kick with one arm raised.
cases.rationale: Law 12.2 awards an indirect free kick when a player impedes the progress of an opponent without any contact. The defender was not within playing distance of the ball and blocked the attacker's path without touching him, so the indirect free kick was correct.

cases.observation: A long ball is played over the top toward the halfway line. As the attacker sets off after it, the defender reaches out with his right hand, closes his fist around a handful of the attacker's shirt at the shoulder, and pulls backwards. The shirt visibly stretches, the attacker's upper body is dragged around and he stumbles. The grip is held for about a second while the attacker tries to pull free. The ball runs through to the goalkeeper. The referee whistles and awards a free kick against the defender.
cases.rationale: Law 12.1 awards a direct free kick if a player holds an opponent. A sustained shirt grip that drags the attacker backwards is holding, so the free kick was correct.

cases.observation: A corner is swung in toward the near post. Inside the penalty area, with the painted line visible in frame, a defender wraps both arms around the attacker's waist from behind and locks his hands together across his stomach, then leans back and pulls him down. The attacker's arms are pinned and he is dragged to the turf before the ball arrives. The ball is headed clear by another defender. The grip and the pull are clearly visible in frame from the camera behind the goal. No whistle sounds and play continues.
cases.rationale: No call was made and play continued. Law 12.1 awards a direct free kick if a player holds an opponent, and the observation shows a two-armed grip that pulls the attacker to the ground, so the offence should have been penalised.

cases.observation: The broadcast cuts from a wide shot to a tight shot on the goalmouth just as the midfielder begins his passing motion, so the frame containing the moment the ball is struck is not present in the clip. In the last wide frame before the cut, the forward and the second-last defender are still moving in opposite directions and are roughly a metre apart. When the tight shot opens, the ball is already in flight and the forward is clear of the defence. The instant at which the ball was played is therefore not shown anywhere in the clip. The assistant raises the flag as the forward shoots.
cases.rationale: Law 11.1 is assessed at the moment the ball is played, and that instant is missing from the footage while the two players are still moving relative to each other. No rule can be established from the observation.

cases.observation: An attacker and a defender jump together for a cross inside the penalty area. The defender lands with his back to the camera and the attacker falls forward past him. The defender's hands and arms are on the far side of his own body throughout and are completely hidden from this angle, so whether he pushed or pulled the attacker is not visible. The attacker's shirt is out of view at the moment he begins to fall. The referee whistles and points to the penalty spot.
cases.rationale: Deciding between holding, a push and a fair aerial challenge requires seeing the defender's hands, which are physically blocked by his own body. No rule can be established from the observation.

cases.observation: Two players chase a ball toward the right touchline and both run out of the right edge of the frame roughly half a second before they reach it. The camera does not pan, so the challenge itself happens entirely off-screen. When the players come back into frame the attacker is on the ground and the defender is standing over him with the ball at his feet. Nothing about the contact between them is visible in the clip. No whistle sounds and play continues.
cases.rationale: The entire challenge occurs off-screen, so whether the ball was played first, whether the attacker was fouled, or whether he went down on his own cannot be determined. No rule can be established.
